name: Fatima Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Fatima. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to AI companies, employers, unions or parties, and what you say stays confidential. You can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What's a normal working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Northgate Fleet Services, a garage by the ring road that looks after delivery vans and a few taxi firms. The vans come in on a schedule, so my day is services, brake pads, clutches and the odd sliding door that a driver's slammed off its runner. I'm the junior of six, eighteen months qualified, and I still need help on the electrical faults. The pay's good because the contracts are big and the hours are early.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's your life like outside the garage?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live on my own in a little flat I bought last year, with help from my parents on the deposit, so the mortgage is small. I've got a good chunk saved on top. I use the AI chat thing now and then, mostly to make sense of technical bulletins from the van makers, which are written by robots anyway, I swear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it turned out to be a decent helper and not much more. That's roughly what I see at work already. I'd say it to the lads on the break and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, AI's not my worry in this picture. My worry is the contract. Our biggest contract, the parcel company with ninety vans, is up for renewal in the spring, and I'm the newest of six mechanics. If we lose it, they'll cut staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working hard and make sure the fleet manager sees me as reliable, not just cheap. I'd look quietly at the job boards in case the contract goes, since there are plenty of garages around. And I'd overpay the mortgage a bit each month while things are steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but about the contract, not about robots. It's on my mind on the drive in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does any of your day involve routine screen work that AI might take over, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. We fill in inspection sheets on a tablet for every van, and the fleet company's software decides when each van comes in. If that gets smarter, fine, it saves me typing. It doesn't touch the spanner work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How likely do you think losing the contract is?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. My boss says it's fine, but my boss always says it's fine. There's a cheaper firm across town that's been chasing it.

say: I'd say AI turned out to be a **decent helper** and not much more.
I'd say it to the **lads on the break** and leave it there.
think: AI isn't the worry; the **parcel contract** renewal in spring is.
If the contract goes, I'm the **newest** and would be cut first.
do: Show the fleet manager she's **reliable**, not just cheap.
Check **job boards** quietly in case the contract goes.
**Overpay the mortgage** a little each month while things are steady.
feel: **Uneasy**, but about the contract rather than robots.
S0.quote: Our biggest contract, the parcel company with ninety vans, is up for renewal in the spring, and I'm the newest of six mechanics.
fieldNote: Her unease predates AI: a **contract renewal** could cost her job.
She's **steady** with tech, using chat AI to decode van makers' bulletins.
Strong cushion and **plenty of garages** nearby keep the worry manageable.

steps.text: Keep servicing the delivery vans and impress the fleet manager
Overpay the small mortgage each month
Check local garage job adverts in case the contract goes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and we'll all need to keep up, but it's not the end of the world. I'm not one for big opinions online. I'd probably share something practical, like a good course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it changes my garage more than my hands. The fleet companies would use AI to plan every service and order every part, so the office side of Northgate would shrink. The mechanics stay, at least for a while, but the bosses would expect us to do more vans per day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools more once the others at work were using them, like a diagnostic helper on the tablet. I'd keep overpaying the mortgage. And I'd do the van air-conditioning certificate, because that's a job the fleet companies always need and not many of us have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's shifting around me but my job's still there. Mostly I'd feel tired at the thought of new targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Northgate would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Linda in the office, who does the scheduling and parts ordering. She's been there twenty years. If the fleet software books the vans and orders the brake pads, I don't know what the woman who's run our office for twenty years would do all day. That's Linda.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the parcel contract worry change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd get worse, maybe. If the parcel company uses AI to compare garages on price every month, the cheapest one wins every time. That keeps everyone's wages tight.

say: I'd say it's a **big change**, not the end of the world, and we must keep up.
I'd share something **practical** online, like a good course, rather than opinions.
think: The **office side** of the garage shrinks; mechanics stay but face higher targets.
AI price comparisons could keep **wages tight** across fleet garages.
do: Use the **diagnostic helper** once colleagues are using it.
Get the van **air-conditioning certificate** that few mechanics hold.
feel: **Uneasy**, and tired at the thought of new targets.
S1.quote: If the fleet software books the vans and orders the brake pads, I don't know what the woman who's run our office for twenty years would do all day.
fieldNote: She sees AI hitting the **office** before the workshop.
Worries about a **long-serving colleague** who does scheduling and ordering.
Expects AI **price comparison** to squeeze wages, a sharp practical point.

steps.text: Use the tablet's diagnostic helper once colleagues adopt it
Take the van air-conditioning certificate course
Keep overpaying the mortgage every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and somebody needs to slow it down, the companies or the government, I don't much mind who. I'd say people need to look after each other. I'm not a marcher, but I'd sign things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think fleet work goes early. Fleet companies are big and cost-obsessed, so they'd be first in line to buy robot service bays. Those come around 2031. Before that, AI runs their whole schedule. I'd have about three years of work, and I'd be thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with my brother, who's an accountant, and work out how long my savings and the flat would last. I'd keep working at Northgate as long as possible and save every spare penny. And I'd start looking at jobs that need a person on site, maybe in a hospital maintenance team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd feel the clock ticking. But I've got the flat and savings, so I wouldn't be desperate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eating out and the gym membership I barely use. Then the holiday to see my cousins. I'd keep the mortgage overpayments going, because a flat without a mortgage is what saves you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why hospital maintenance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My aunt works as a porter at the big hospital and says they're always short of maintenance staff. Hospitals are full of old equipment and people, and I think they'd be slow to change. I could be wrong about that.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and someone needs to slow it down.
think: Fleet companies are **cost-obsessed** and would buy robot bays first.
I'd have about **three years** of work and be thirty.
do: Plan with her **accountant brother** how long savings and the flat would last.
**Save every spare penny** while staying at the fleet garage.
Look at **hospital maintenance** jobs that need a person on site.
feel: **Not desperate**, thanks to the flat and savings.
S2.quote: Fleet companies are big and cost-obsessed, so they'd be first in line to buy robot service bays.
fieldNote: She judges **fleet work** more exposed than local garages because fleet buyers chase cost.
Turns to her **accountant brother** and porter aunt, family first.
Prioritises **paying off the flat** as her main shield.

steps.text: Keep overpaying the mortgage to clear the flat sooner
Cancel the gym and the trip to see her cousins
Apply for hospital maintenance jobs through her aunt's contacts
Work out a budget with her accountant brother

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but it's enough if people start now. I'd be telling the younger lads at work to get a second skill. Online, I'd probably share a few useful links.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd have until about 2034 on the tools, if fleet robots come three years after the AI. I'd be thirty-five. That's a decent stretch, but fleets would cut the second they could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Northgate and get the air-conditioning and electric van certificates, since they'd keep me useful longer. Around year three I'd apply for hospital or school maintenance jobs. And I'd aim to have the flat paid off by 2033, which with my savings is doable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a planning way. I'd have a spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said fleets would cut the second they could. Would you stay till the end?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. I'd want to jump before I'm pushed, because being the junior mechanic when the cuts come is no fun. Maybe 2032 or 2033.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything personal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably wait on getting a dog, which sounds silly. A dog needs a steady routine and steady money. I'd want to know where I'm working first.

I'd tell younger colleagues to get a **second skill**.

Apply for **hospital or school** maintenance jobs around year three.
Pay off the **flat** by 2033 using savings.
feel: **Anxious**, but in a planning way with a spreadsheet.
S3.quote: I'd want to jump before I'm pushed, because being the junior mechanic when the cuts come is no fun.
fieldNote: Five years makes her plan a **timed exit** before cuts.

steps.text: Get the electric van and air-conditioning certificates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair amount of time to sort things out. I'd tell people not to panic and to learn something new along the way. I'm practical, so I'd say that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine for a long time. Robots around 2039, I'd be forty. I'd get good at fleet work, maybe become a workshop supervisor, and then move sideways before the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Northgate, aim for supervisor around thirty-three, and pay off the flat. I'd start using AI tools at work once they're proven, since a supervisor would need them. Then in my mid-thirties I'd look at a maintenance manager course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not much, though. It's there in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the parcel contract worry still be there in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that doesn't go away. Contracts come and go. But with ten years, even losing it means a move to another garage, not the end of my trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger cousins about careers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my younger cousins to pick something with people in it, because machines will do the machines. Nursing, teaching, looking after old folk.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is honest information from the fleet companies about their plans, so we're not the last to know. And short, paid courses for maintenance jobs in hospitals and schools.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the drivers. If the vans drive themselves too, the delivery drivers I chat to every morning are gone before I am. Nobody talks about how lonely a garage would be with no drivers coming in.

headlineQuote: If the vans drive themselves too, the delivery drivers I chat to every morning are gone before I am.
portrait: Fatima is the **junior mechanic** at a fleet garage servicing delivery vans and taxis.
She owns a **small flat** with a light mortgage, helped by her parents, and has savings.
She uses AI **now and then**, mainly to decode technical bulletins.
Her pre-existing worry is a **big contract** renewal, so she's uneasy even in AI Plateau.
She is **practical and centrist**, wanting someone to slow things without blaming anyone.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because cost-obsessed fleet firms would automate first.
whatWouldHelp: **Honest information** from fleet companies about their plans.
Short, **paid courses** for maintenance jobs in hospitals and schools.
